en.title: The Wildest Video Game Budgets Can't Hold A Candle To GTA 6
en.description: The latest Grand Theft Auto is thought to be the most expensive entertainment product ever made.
en.fullContent:
The latest Grand Theft Auto is thought to be the most expensive entertainment product ever made.

When you think about the most expensive entertainment productions ever created, video games are likely not the first thing that comes to mind. Hollywood studios routinely spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a single movie that can have a multi-year production schedule. But video games have actually become just as expensive to produce of late, sometimes even surpassing major films. Case in point: Grand Theft Auto VI looks set to become the most expensive game ever created.

While Rockstar Games hasn't publicly disclosed how much it has spent so far, analysts peg the estimated budget at well over $1 billion, with some putting the current figure at around $1.5 billion. That puts GTA VI in rarefied territory, as it outpaces the known budgets of both major theatrical releases and other AAA games. So what has caused video game development to become so expensive and why is GTA VI's budget in particular eclipsing other big names?

A billion-dollar video game budget may seem surprising at first glance, but it starts to make sense once you consider that a modern game often has just as many moving pieces as a Hollywood production. You need actors, writers, programmers, animators, designers and composers among others to make an expansive open-world game. And short of a few outliers like the Avatar series, movies are typically in active production for a couple of years. GTA VI has been in active development for closer to a decade. Once a game is nearing completion, it usually goes through a rigorous testing process that requires yet another team.

Apart from a handful of indie breakthroughs, it's common for game budgets to quickly spiral into the double or triple-digit millions these days. Game development can also take several years, with hundreds of employees dedicated to a single project.

Development costs and timelines have been steadily rising, though. In 2023, court documents revealed that Sony Interactive Entertainment had spent $212 million on Horizon Forbidden West and $220 million on The Last of Us: Part II.

en.title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026
en.description: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine ...
en.fullContent:
There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
  See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations here

After 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.
  4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox

Billed as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.
  10 September; PC, PS5, Xbox

The team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.
  15 September; PS5

The tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimed Fire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.
   17 September; Switch 2

Silent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …
  24 September; PC, PS5

en.title: 5 Best Super Mario Video Games Of All Time, Ranked
en.description: After helping Nintendo gain traction in the global gaming industry as the protagonist of its breakout hit "Donkey Kong," Mario went on to become th...
en.fullContent:
After helping Nintendo gain traction in the global gaming industry as the protagonist of its breakout hit "Donkey Kong," Mario went on to become the company's enduring mascot. This was only elevated with the landmark 1985 title "Super Mario Bros.," a tremendous hit for the Nintendo Entertainment System and a retro game everyone needs to play. This spawned the "Super Mario" series, a franchise of games starring Mario and his usual cast of supporting characters, typically up against Bowser and his latest scheme to kidnap Princess Peach. The series successfully made the leap to 3D in 1996 with "Super Mario 64" and has featured a mix of 3D and 2D platforming ever since.

To clarify, this list focuses on the "Super Mario" series, not just any video game that happens to star Mario and his friends as playable characters. That means series like "Mario Kart" or "Paper Mario" are not included in this specific article. A "Super Mario" game is a title that emphasizes platforming, whether it be from a side-scrolling or 3D perspective. These are the five best "Super Mario" video games of all time, ranked, featuring Nintendo's flagship character at the height of his powers.

For as long as the Switch was Nintendo's premier home console, it only got a single 3D "Super Mario" game, not counting remasters and re-releases. This title is 2017's "Super Mario Odyssey," which presents its own twist on the familiar Mario out to rescue Peach from Bowser premise. Mario teams up with Cappy, a sentient hat, which he can use in a variety of different ways, including temporarily possessing the different creatures that he flings it onto. Mario collects Power Moons to fuel his airship and pursue Bowser in time to stop him from forcibly marrying Peach.

"Super Mario Odyssey" is a game that justifies the price of the Switch, reminding fans that the series still thrills in 3D, rather than just being a hallmark of its resurgent line of 2D platformers. The 3D platforming is as intuitive as ever and, for an early Switch title, the game still looks great. The game also marks a shift back to wider worlds with multiple objectives and collectibles rather than a more self-contained level format, which it utilizes to fantastic effect. Nearly a decade on, there still isn't a proper sequel to "Super Mario Odyssey," making the game the most recent 3D platformer in the series to date.

When it comes to classic side-scrolling "Super Mario" games on the series' original platform, there's no topping "Super Mario Bros. 3." Released in 1988, the game uses the usual 2D platforming that made its predecessors so memorably enjoyable. But the title also pushes the NES hardware as far as it can go, with more detailed sprites and environments, along with a whole assortment of power-ups. The game also doubles down on its secrets, including numerous hidden exits and warps for players to discover.

Producer, co-director, and co-designer Shigeru Miyamoto was embarrassed by "Super Mario Bros. 3" reportedly, feeling it had aged poorly in comparison to its counterparts. We have to respectfully disagree, with the game's ambitions still admirable and largely effective, with imaginative level design and improved handling. This is all elevated by a lush soundtrack composed by Koji Kondo, solidifying the game's distinctly playful personality. One of the best NES games ever made, "Super Mario Bros. 3" showcases how far the series had grown since its roots only three years prior.

en.title: NBA 2K27 Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
en.description: NBA 2K27 from developer Visual Concepts is another effort in the series aimed at walking the tightrope between modern upgrades and catering to play...
en.fullContent:
NBA 2K27 from developer Visual Concepts is another effort in the series aimed at walking the tightrope between modern upgrades and catering to player feedback.

It's a tough balance to seek, no doubt. Last year's game kept pushing things in realistic directions on and off the court, while also listening to player feedback when it comes to shot meters and specific systems.

This year? More of the same, in a good way, with a push to get more realistic-feeling things on the court and finer control over the many systems off it.

The best entry yet thing is starting to become a cliché, sure, but NBA 2K27 has a shot at it once more thanks to measured upgrades atop a strong foundation.

One glance says the gameplay in NBA 2K27 is a leap. There's obvious new cutoff angles and droves of more dynamic animations, at the hoop amid contact or otherwise.

The strive for freshness and realism this year takes a Shai Gilgeous-Alexander slant with the long-awaited inclusion of the step-through up-and-under, which adds a more dynamic option to the gameplay, for the ball-handler and defender alike.

en.title: Massive 12TB Steam leak reveals decades of unreleased games — archived files include unseen Half-Life 2: Episode 3 builds and assets
en.description: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.
en.fullContent:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Valve might've just suffered its biggest data leak in history, but it wasn't a hack or a security breach. Instead, the company left an endpoint to its legacy infrastructure accessible to the public, from where archivists extracted 12-13TB of old game content. The files are still being explored, but we know they include both Valve's internal projects and third-party releases, with an early weapon asset from Half-Life 2 Episode 3 being the key discovery, along with scrapped Portal 2 concepts.

The archive consists of old Steam content-server data from 2003 to 2013, overlapping with the timeline of the platform's upgrade from the old Steam2 system to SteamPipe. Valve used to distribute games via proprietary NCF (No-Cache File) and GCF (Grid Cache File) formats during the Steam2 era before it transitioned to a standard HTTP file-tree system around March 2013. Therefore, this dump basically acts like a preserved time capsule.

During this period, Valve was a much more active game developer, so we get a rare insight into their projects. First up is Left 4 Dead, and the files include an entire early build of the game from June 2008. It has a different HUD, different voice lines cut from the retail release, altered sections of the map, and many unfinished early assets that Valve was recycling from the Terror Strike mod (for Counter-Strike: Condition Zero).

left 4 dead 2 beta dead center map #2the exterior outside of the hotel leads you across the street instead of right, directly to the gunstore.this is like whiplash nothing is the same, its like a dream sequence of what im used to pic.twitter.com/AIcvykRe80August 30, 2026

Then, there's Portal 2, which is actually said to have been hit the hardest, and modders have similarly reconstructed a playable build from the files. It's a beta dating back to July 2009 when the game was still in its Core Hub era before that concept was scrapped in favor of a more direct sequel. We also get to see early assets from the F-Stop prequel that was in development the year prior, featuring camera mechanics for gameplay.
